utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we have the witness, are there any submissions? Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Prosecution has two oral applications. The first one concerns an application in relation to the six remaining 92 bis witnesses. As the Court knows, initially we had eight 92 bis witnesses on our list. There are now six remaining. What we are -- what we would like to do is all of -- is take all of them except one, Mr. Zebic, who is scheduled to testify tomorrow -- take all of them except Zebic and use those witnesses as 89(F) witnesses. It is a very similar procedure, and the 89(F) process has been used in this case, as the Court knows. It's been used in the Limaj case, in the Krajisnik case. It's been used in the Milosevic case. It has been authorised by the Appellate Chamber. And we would like to 89(F) those witnesses in the same manner that we would do them under 92 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I wonder whether any of those witnesses are intending to have some protective measures because, you know, I might ask for the response from the Defence, and Defence counsel may deal with them one by one by mentioning their names. So I wonder whether we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As a protection, I think we should go to the private session. At this point, I don't believe any of them will be asking for protective measures. However, some witnesses when they arrive here do explain some sort of change of circumstances and make that request upon arrival. So maybe as a protective measures we should go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrissey, any response? If you are going to deal with those witnesses one by one, we should go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not in a position to deal with them one by one yet. We only received notice of this application this morning. We're busy with other things, and we're just not ready to respond, I'm sorry to say. It is necessary to respond on a case-by-case basis. There may be among these witnesses one or more who are appropriate to deal with on this basis, and there may be some who aren't. There's one, at least, in my mind who I -- I haven't had time to research it or to reread that person's statement yet, but I'd be very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we have a technical problem. Maybe you could try it again, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the transcript captured the words I had to say up to now, but I'll recommence. Your Honours, we're into the ready to deal with this application on a case-by-case basis. It should be dealt with on a case-by-case --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The LiveNote is not working here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the crushing inequality of arms that affects the Prosecutor seems to be working because it's working very well for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Should I say the word "testing" to see if it emerges on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have two that are functioning, so we can continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If the Prosecution is comfortable, I'll proceed. Are you okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. Your Honours, first of all, this application really needs to be brought with more notice to the Defence. I'm not sure what position the Chamber finds itself in, but the Defence, we received notice of this application this morning. And it's -- it raises issues of law and it raises, frankly, issues of differentiation between the witnesses. So it's not a matter we're -- I'm even able to respond yet, I'm sorry to say. I don't mean to be obstructionist about it, but that's the position we're in. This application has just come on rather suddenly, from the Defence point of view, and we can't answer it. We can't say what our position is in respect of each witness. I can say in general terms a couple of things: We would be against any general ruling. It should be done on a case-by-case basis, of course. Each witness has their own story to tell and each witness may have something controversial or less controversial to say. So from that point of view, I'm not -- we don't -- we certainly don't support this application, but I'd like some time actually to consider how we deal with it. It's not desirable to delay these matters. I fully understand that. But we're just -- we're just not ready, unfortunately. Now, I understand the Prosecutor's second motion may concern Mr. -- one of these very witnesses. I'm just not sure about that, but I think that is the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. Could I ask you -- when will you be ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what we -- what occurred to me as a helpful way of dealing with it would be that the Prosecutor could put a brief written submission about this. Because it does involve some matters of principle and because it deals with witnesses whose stories differ - I don't mean from each other, but each one gives evidence about something quite different - that the Prosecution, if they were able to put this matter in a sensible written submission -- it doesn't have to be lengthy, but it needs to spell out why it is that it's in the interests of justice to take this step. It can't be about saving time because the witness Zebic, they're proposing not to use that process with him. They may have good reasons for doing what they're doing in respect of Zebic. Frankly, I haven't -- I haven't even looked at the proofing notes for Zebic yet, because we just got those this morning. But whatever the interests of justice may be, it ought to be justified in a sensible way and give the Defence an opportunity to respond. We don't need long. And frankly, Your Honours, we'd respond on -- on Thursday. If we could receive something tomorrow, we'd respond immediately. But it can't be -- we can't be rushed like this. I've been preparing Mr. Okovic this morning. That's really what I've been doing. I feel a bit embarrassed to be inarticulate about it right now, but that's because I'm caught on the hop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it is our original plan to do everything orally or in the simplest way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we will hear Mr. Weiner on this issue, whether you're in the position to submit some very short submissions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. If -- if you would like it in writing, we can do it in writing; if not, I can do it orally. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe Mr. Morrissey would like to have it in writing, but not the Trial Chamber. But since there is a request from the Defence, would you please submit your written submissions on that effect, but keep it as concise as possible and file it tomorrow so that Mr. Morrissey could deal with it on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How about the next issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The next one is much simpler, and it is a joint motion between the Defence and the Prosecution. Your Honour, at this point we are scheduled to return to court after the holiday on the 29th, which is the Tuesday after Easter Monday. Since there will be witnesses flying in to testify later in the week and since it is a holiday - both Sunday and Monday are holidays - it has been done in the past and we would be making a request in this case that we could start on Wednesday; therefore, when witnesses fly in, they will not have to be picked up during the holiday, that people don't have to go out and talk to them during the holiday. So it would be easier for both the Victim and Witnesses Unit in going to the airport, transporting witnesses; it's easier for us to get witnesses in on the Tuesday than the weekend; it's less difficult to get people when it's not a holiday; and it's also easier because when they come in, the Prosecution generally meets them on that day. It's easier for the Prosecution not to come in and meet them on the holiday. So we would request that trial begin on the 30th. That way the witnesses could arrive on the 29th, we could meet with any new witnesses, and continue on the 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is there anything to add, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. The Defence joins in that request. It will assist us in terms of proofing notes and the like so that we -- we join in that request as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultations with my colleagues and based on the joint submission by both parties, we decided that we will continue the proceedings on the 30th of March so that the -- both parties will have enough time to prepare for the witnesses coming that week. It is so decided. And there's another announcement: That for this week's sitting, on Thursday and Friday we will sit in the morning session instead of the afternoon. Yes. And I believe that the next witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There is another matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness is Mr. Kemo Kapur. My learned colleague Mr. Weiner said there is another issue and that's relating to the use of 89(F) with that witness. I'm not sure whether we actually made a formal application. The Prosecution certainly spoke to our Defence colleagues last week, and I understand that there was no difficulty with that particular witness giving his evidence via the provisions of 89(F), he being one of the witnesses who was on the Rule 92 bis list before. On the list that we submitted last week, we originally had Mr. Kapur to give his evidence later in the week. However, he is in fact a serving judge of the lower court in Sarajevo and is basically needed back at work as soon as possible. And when he arrived yesterday, we asked -- we spoke to the Defence and asked if we could move him forward to accommodate his judicial duties in Sarajevo. And the Prosecution proposes to lead his evidence by -- by way of Rule 89(F) and makes the application that it be done so in the interests of justice. The statement doesn't go to the acts or conduct of the accused. We have prepared an eight-page new statement which combines the salient features and relevant features of his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in December -- sorry, in 2000, and some parts of the statement he made to the military security service in December 1993, and there is very minor additional matter which arose right out of proofing yesterday, and it is simply this: The witness -- and it is in his statement, and I've discussed this with my learned colleague. The witness says that he was the chief of military police for the 9th Motorised Brigade. He says every morning there were daily meetings in the command headquarters of all the subordinate commanders, and on one day in 1993 - he doesn't know when - Mr. Halilovic attended the meeting for about half an hour and, apart from exchanging pleasantries, didn't say anything else. That's the only reference to the accused, Mr. Halilovic, in the entire statement. Now, I understand from discussions with Defence that until that last matter was raised, there was no opposition to the use of 89(F). I understand that they were seeking instructions from their client in the extended delay because of the technical problems, and I don't know what the situation is at the moment. The Prosecution's submission is this is a witness who is basically uncontroversial, who provides evidence about the activities of the 9th in Sarajevo before September 1993. Your Honours have been provided with a copy of the proposed 89(F) statement. In reality, it will take -- to lead that evidence orally, it will probably take maybe two hours or so to do so. To lead the evidence by way of 89(F), it will take basically a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, there is, Your Honour. We don't -- we don't consent to this. We oppose it being done. Your Honours, there was -- there were discussions last week. I might prefer to leave of discussions that happened between counsel outside of the court and just leave -- leave the Court with the submissions to deal with. But we were provided today with the Bosnian version of the proofing notes by email at around midday, perhaps a little after midday. Because of the situation that exists in the Defence room, it took us time to have that printed because there was a lengthy Milosevic document being printed, so that upon attending in court today, Mr. Halilovic was shown this document for the first time in Bosnian. Now, we -- the Defence is -- is prepared to cooperate to the best of our ability in these matters. We don't want to keep the person from their duties needlessly. It seemed to me an appropriate compromise was this: That the witness Okovic should proceed now; he should proceed first, as he was going to do, as we've all thought he was going to do,. We'd be prepared to accommodate the other witness, Mr. Kapur, shortly afterwards, but that, of course, is subject to the rulings, the 89(F) rulings that Your Honours must make. It may be that overnight we could give some thought to an expedited response to the Prosecution's wishes in relation to Mr. Kapur. It may that be we could hurry that up and we could respond tomorrow morning in terms of the 89(F) component of all of that. For myself -- Mr. Mettraux is the person concerned with taking that witness, but we wouldn't object to Mr. Kapur being imposed after this witness. That, we think, would give us time. But frankly, our plans were based on a different schedule, so that we weren't ready. You know, we don't want to embarrass this witness, but these applications, they've got to -- they've got to be made earlier. In this case, the Prosecutor's provided us with details, and we couldn't really give a final version of what we wanted to say until after we had the proofing notes and the statement. We've got them now. I've got some concerns about it, frankly, myself. We don't -- we don't consent it to that being done, and we submit that what should happen is that Mr. Okovic should proceed. We would be prepared to talk to the Prosecutor further overnight. It may be we could resolve the 89(F) issue orally first thing in the morning -- or first thing in tomorrow's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just note two things I neglected to say before: First, we actually provided the Defence with the 89(F) statement which you have before you at the moment last night - I think at about 7.00 or so - with a very minor change to it this morning. The witness approved it yesterday. We actually went to a fair amount of trouble to have a Bosnian version translated and prepared for the Defence today. There's no requirement for us to provide the Defence with a Bosnian version, but we have provided two identical signed versions, one in English and one in Bosnian, and the Defence have been on notice of the entirety of the statement since last night, and there's nothing new in the statement, apart from the -- apart from the statement that Mr. Halilovic attended a meeting for half an hour one morning. So in my respectful submission, the Defence aren't taken by surprise because the evidence is exactly what the witness would have -- what we would have led from the witness anyway from his statement to the OTP and some parts from his earlier statement. There's nothing knew there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I'll have to respond to that. Your Honours, up until yesterday, there was nothing to suggest that Sefer Halilovic had been in the company of this witness at a meeting. Now, after 11 years or so, we learn -- you know, at this time, we -- for some reason we learn about -- that the Prosecution are proposing to lead evidence that he was. Now, that's new. It's -- given my friend's explanation, it may not be that significant, as he's explained it. But as Your Honours have received that statement, you'll see that the way it's phrased is rather ambiguous. You see, it doesn't make it clear that he didn't take part in any discussions. The proofing -- the note that you've got says that there used to be discussions of -- of all sorts of matters, including criminal type of matters, and that Mr. Halilovic was there. And it's all in the same -- it was originally, at least in the version we were given at first, all in the same paragraph. So it looked rather as if it was being suggested that Mr. Halilovic was privy to such discussions. That's how the note looked. Now, the new version of it that we've received today - and that's what I'm talking about, the final version - seems to clarify that to a degree, but it's a matter that concerns Mr. Halilovic. And to be rushed into it like this with an hour's notice is a practice that shouldn't be encouraged. It shouldn't -- you know, we're prepared to deal on a case-by-case basis with anything. But when a witness is ready to be dealt with on Wednesday or Thursday, it upsets the preparation; it causes problems. So a compromise seems to me to be the one I've suggested. That seems to me to be a way of accommodating the witness and allowing him to go back soon, as soon as possible, not to put him back to the end of the week, where he was supposed to be. But right now we -- we have new information. We'd like the time. Mr. Halilovic has only just read the material. And when I say he's read it, he's been provided it. I don't even know if he has read it yet, because as I provided it to him and explained what was happening, we were summoned into court. So that's how we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, could I ask you a question. What was the time frame for that meeting in which the witness saw Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's 1993, when he was Chief of Staff. The witness cannot be more specific. The -- I discussed this with my learned friend in some detail. The witness will say there was a meeting. There's a daily meeting every morning of the brigade, and Mr. Halilovic attended one on one occasion only. He was there for about half an hour. The witness does not remember what was discussed. As far as he remembers, Mr. Halilovic was silent, apart from exchanging pleasantries. And that is as far as we take it. That will be his evidence on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if we have, you know, so many things unclear, what's the purpose for you to introduce this kind of material into evidence at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if, you know, his statement -- you know, there are a lot of things that are unclear, then what is the purpose for you to introduce this kind of evidence? I mean concerned with the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution case is that Mr. Halilovic had a relationship with Celo, Ramiz Delalic, who was the deputy commander of the brigade, and that there is evidence from other witnesses about communications between the two of them. This small piece of evidence may be corroborative of that by the fact that he attended a meeting. But on the other hand, we of course recognise that we don't know where Mr. Halilovic was the rest of the time. He may well have been attending brigade meetings on a daily basis throughout Sarajevo or Bosnia, we don't know. But it does corroborate a small part of the Prosecution evidence. That's as far as we take it. We don't seek to put it any higher than that other than to say he attended a brigade meeting one morning which corroborates to a small extent the fact that he had a relationship with Mr. Delalic. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you are going to consider the counter-suggestion put forward by Mr. Morrissey that we'll hear Mr. Okovic and tomorrow we'll hear this 89(F) witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution is in the Trial Chamber's hands on that. If the Defence feels that it has not had time to take instructions on whether or not Mr. Halilovic attended that particular meeting and whether it has any significance to their defence and isn't in a position to deal with that today, I understand. Although I do say we did inform them of this last night, we're in the Trial Chamber's hands, and if the Trial Chamber thinks it preferable to call Mr. Okovic first, we will accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultation with my colleagues, the Bench decided that we will hear Mr. Okovic first for today, and then tomorrow we'll come to that 89(f) witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're grateful for that indication. Could I indicate we'd be prepared to expedite the 89(F) argument generally. I don't know if the Prosecutor can -- can do this, but if they could get something to us of any sort this evening, we would -- we'd produce our response tomorrow morning so that the 89(F) issue could proceed in an orderly way. We're happy to do that although we asked for two days. It may be too soon for the Prosecutors, I don't know, but if they can -- if they can give us something night we'll respond tomorrow which might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, could I have Mr. Okovic. Is he available now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okovic should be available. If you could give me -- give us a couple minutes, maybe a five-minute break we'll find Mr. Okovic, and also Attorney Chana will be leading that evidence. So we would get her down from the third floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will have ten minutes' break and we'll resume at ten minutes past three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you give us your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zakir Okovic. I was born on the 6th of November, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will lead the witness on his personal particulars with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Okovic, in 1986 you graduated in physics from Sarajevo University; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And before the outbreak of the war, you lived in Sarajevo where you worked as the director of Zaks firm?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: From 1980 to 1981, you served as a private in a JNA air force unit. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: On 4 April 1992, you joined the TO in the municipality of Stari Grad, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You then joined a military police unit which was under the command of Dzevad Topic, and you stayed there for about five to six months.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: After that, you became a member of the Solakovic Battalion of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Okovic, who was the deputy battalion commander of this unit?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Samir Pezo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the security chief -- the chief of security assigned to this particular corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that man only by nickname. His nickname was Pike. I cannot recall his real name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okovic. And who was the chief of security of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Sacir Arnautovic or something like that. I'm not absolutely sure. At that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was your job in the Solakovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I usually prepared offensive actions in the unit and led those actions without any other order but the personal order of my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Solakovic, Mr. Solakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the first name, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Adnan Solakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was your title? What was your title in this unit?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Operations officer for combat activities or something like that. In that unit, there were no strict orders as to who was doing what job.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Okovic, I will now ask you to cast your mind to early September 1993. Can you tell us any event which happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: In early September, my commander was summoned to the command of the 1st Corps, and as I was in charge of offensive actions at the line, the commander said I was to accompany him. We arrived at the meeting in the command of the 1st Corps or, rather, in the office of the corps commander, Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who else was present when you arrived at this office?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: There was Mr. Sefer Halilovic in the office also.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: The corps commander, Vahid Karavelic, commander of the 1st Corps, my immediate commander Adnan Solakovic, and I think -- I can't really remember, but I think that Pike was there, too, as the security man.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Solakovic, can you give a date to this meeting, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the precise date, but I think it was one or two days before the trip to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what date would that be, if you remember the trip to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 9th, the 9th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Are you sure of that date?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. As we go along, perhaps you'll remind yourself. Now, what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, Mr. Halilovic explained the significance of the operation that was being carried out in Herzegovina. He said that Mostar was under siege and the siege had to be lifted. He insisted that our unit be sent to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what kind of operations were these?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: These were classical combat operations, practically to liberate part of the territory in order to make life easier in Mostar, which was encircled. It was to liberate the line we were attacking in order to create an open communication to Mostar and to break the encirclement of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what exactly was Mr. Halilovic asking for, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic only insisted that our unit participate in these offensive actions, at least according to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was Vahid Karavelic's view on the matter?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think at that point in time, when all the units able to intervene in the Sarajevo war theatre, which was very unstable at the time-- he was reluctant to agree to what Mr. Halilovic was asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what transpired?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my feeling, that he was unwilling to let our unit leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why was he unwilling to let your unit leave the town? What were the considerations placed on the table, as it were, at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the town would be left without an intervention unit able to act at the front line defending the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were your units holding part of the front line in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Our unit was an intervention unit of the 1st Corps. It would intervene where the line was under threat, where it was about to fall, and in similar situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what was the conclusion at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: The final conclusion was that an order should be issued that our unit was to be sent to carry out the operation in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And after you got this order for you to go, how many of you were prepared to go to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object to that. The witness gave an answer a minute ago and he said that the conclusion was that an order should be issued. Now, it may be that in due course he did receive an order, but that should be established before we jump forward to what happened as a result of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the Prosecution did not believe that is important for that order, but you have the full right to cross this witness on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Most obliged, Your Honour. I will -- for the sake of completeness:

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was such an order issued, Mr. Okovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see such an order. It was taken over by my commander. I received an order from my commander that I should prepare the unit to set out.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you tell me who eventually decided that these -- your units will be going to Herzegovina? Whose decision was it?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Karavelic. He was the corps commander. He had to make the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you know from whom this order came?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that because I was not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. But what were you required to do? What were you asked to do by Mr. Karavelic immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: To prepare the unit to get moving and on the following day to set out to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, which commanders were to go with you as you were going to set out to go to Herzegovina, other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. So what day was it that you set out to go to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think we set out on the 9th of September, but I'm not sure of the date. It was one day after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if I show you a document which might assist you with some of the dates, Mr. Okovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show the witness -- which 65 ter is 78, which would be 01083147. May I give the Bosnian copy to the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Okovic, could you tell us what is this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: This document is a report on combat activities of the unit in the period from the 8th to the 19th of September, and it was compiled after the return of the unit to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the date it was compiled was the 25th September 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is this a report you compiled after you came back from your mission to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Although I wanted to keep in chronological order, I'm showing you this document so you may -- may look at it and see the notations you made at the time and especially about the dates, and then I will ask you this question again as to when you set out for Herzegovina and perhaps the document will help you, but I will talk about the document later. When did you -- when did --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just going to add -- I don't have any -- any objection to the witness refreshing his memory from this document, if -- if that would assist matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us now, after refreshing your memory with this particular document, when was it that you set out for Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I signed the document, I can see from it that we set out on the 8th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who came along with you as you set out?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I was the leader of the trip, and I was commanding the unit as it travelled to Herzegovina. With me were the company commander and the lower-level commanders of the subordinate units, logistics men and so on. There was no one else from my command apart from myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how many soldiers accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact number, but I think it was about -- well, less than a hundred men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the unit from the beginning to the end of the war remained multi-ethnic. There were also Serbs, Croats, Roma, Jews, but of course most of the men were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this document, Mr. Okovic, it says: "Pursuant to the order of the 1st Corps commander of 7 September 1993, a company of 125 soldiers were prepared for sending in the area of Jablanica. At 2130 hours the company was transferred through the DB object in the region of Butmir." Would that be correct that you set out at night at 2130 on the 7th of September, as reflected in your -- in your report?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: This is probably correct, because I drew up this report based on my notes, and I remember it was night. The soldiers passed through the tunnel at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what time did you arrive in the morning to your destination, and what was that destination?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, we arrived at Jablanica. Early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Zuka waited for us in Jablanica. He was the commander of the Zulfikar detachment. He gave me a logistics man of his, who took us to Grabovica, to the village of Grabovica, and he took us to where we were going to be camped.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why did you report to Zuka, Alispago Zulfikar?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's what it said in the order on our departure for Herzegovina, and it was his area of responsibility anyway, so he was the one who was providing logistical support for us, accommodation, food for the soldiers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, this would be on the 8th of September; right? We just -- I want to make sure that our dates are quite clear as we move along. So where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We went to the village of Grabovica, and we took up two empty houses. This is where the soldiers were billeted. And I set up a command at the old railway station building. That's where the railway station used to be. That was the building where I set up the command at.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Grabovica, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: People. In the sense of people.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were accommodated on the right bank of the Neretva River. I think this was populated by Croat citizens. It was 100 per cent Croat, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this is on the right side of the Neretva, did you say?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In a minute I'm going to show you -- I'm going to show you a photograph, Mr. Okovic, and I'd like you to identify which of the -- which house that you were billeted in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could P3 be put on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was on the other side of the river, the side that you were not billeted on?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We were accommodated in this area here. On the other side of the river, there were some prefabricated huts for workers, and that's where refugees were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Okovic, I want you to take that pen, please, which is being offered to you, and would you mark where you were billeted first, and put a "1" and then circle that "1," would you.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: My unit was billeted there. On this side, I think in these prefabricated huts, the refugees were accommodated -- Muslim refugees. That's marked with the number "3." And then on the photograph you can't see the place where -- this was just before the turning for Mostar. This is where Cedo's Wolves unit was accommodated. That's somewhere around here, but you cannot actually see it on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is that the corner there, with the little red dot there? Could you just draw an arrow away from there --

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- please and put a "4" there.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's take number 1. That's where you were billeted. And could you tell us who was billeted in this particular house where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot really see it very well here. This has been rebuilt, restored. The house is probably still there, but it's now covered with the foliage from trees and so on. We found two Muslim refugees from Stolac who were living in that house together with a Croat couple, and we found them in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how old was this Croat couple that you found in the house?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they were in their 60s.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So how many soldiers were in the house which you have marked "1" on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We were using just one room. How shall I put it? It was on the south side of the house. The other rooms were being used by those refugees, the two refugees, and the couple. Later, because we were short of space, I asked if it would be possible for them to let us use one more room, which they did later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what about number 2, where you marked the circle? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: That house was empty, and that's where the members of the unit that I belonged to were billeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How many soldiers are we talking about in that house?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: You could see one more house. You cannot see it on this picture. It was sort of semi-knocked down, that house, and the rest of the soldiers from our unit were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, these two Muslim refugees from Stolac, were they men or women?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: They were middle-aged men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So -- thank you for this. Thank you very much for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to introduce that into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what did you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P271, and the previous document that was shown with ERN 0108-3147 is marked MFI270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell the Court what you did on that day.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I deployed the unit to a day of rest that day, and practically that's how we spent the day, resting and waiting to start implementation of our task.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did somebody arrive or some people arrive in Grabovica on the 8th? 7

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of military personnel or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Military personnel.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At around noon, the camp where we where was toured by Vehbija Karic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And anybody else with Vehbija Karic?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Zicro Suljevic and Mr. Bilajac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who were these three men?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, they were members of the Main Staff of the B and H army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what happened once these -- when these men came?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: My first question was, "What do I need to do?" I wanted to have a specific task. I wanted to prepare the unit for the implementation of the task. I asked for the map. I asked for information in order to prepare for the implementation of the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did they come to discuss the assignment or did they come for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: They came to see the unit, whether it was prepared to carry out the task. I tried to explain that -- actually they tried to explain how this whole operation would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what exactly did they say in that -- to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of implementing the task, I asked for the map, for information about the enemy, which they did not have on them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was anything agreed at this particular time, before they went?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: When they did not provide the information about the enemy strength, lines, the map, where the enemy was located, I insisted on some kind of reconnaissance so that we could see what we were attacking, where we were attacking, to prepare for the implementation of the assignment. So they accepted that, and they said that they would pass this on up the chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And "up the chain," what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: To the higher command. Probably to a more superior officer probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was your understanding as to who was their superior officer?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I understood it to mean, since Mr. Halilovic was the most senior officer of the B and H army there, that they had to talk to him. That is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what -- how long did this meeting last?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Not longer than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do after?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I think that they told me that a reporting session was scheduled in Konjic and that somebody would come and that I should attend this briefing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So did you attend this briefing?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what time did you leave for Konjic?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time, but it was already dark. It was already night.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where did you go in Konjic for this meeting -- this briefing?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it used to be a factory or something, in the centre of town. We were -- we went to some conference room or hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was present at this briefing?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer and all the ones that I mentioned before: Karic, Bilajac, Zicro. I think they were there too. Mr. Gusic was there. Mr. Alispago was there. And the commanders from local units were also present. I didn't know any of them. I think that the chief of the Konjic municipality was also there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So how many people would that be all in all?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were more than 12 people there. I'm not sure about the number though.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that to be a preparatory meeting for the implementation of the assignment, and the contents of the discussions were on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were there any assignments given?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who were they given by?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: The tasks were already prepared, as far as I understood, and they were just read out on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who read them out?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was someone from the Main Staff, one of the senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was the most senior officer there?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer. He had the highest rank and he was practically conducting the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you discuss subordination of units and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you discuss in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: My unit was to be resubordinated to Mr. Zulfikar's command because he was issuing orders specifically for that axis along which we were supposed to act.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what would this axis be?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Vrdi axis. That was the name of the village, or Antena, because there are some kind of TV aerials, antennas there also. I don't remember. That was the axis of attack for the unit to which I belonged.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who else was going to be part of this particular axis, the combat on this axis?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: It was only then that I heard that we would be resubordinated under Mr. Alispago's command. These were members of the 9th and the 10th Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was Zuka's unit or Zuka himself subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably to the commander of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the operation?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, that was the most senior-ranking officer who was there, but I don't know who that was under orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you clarify that? And I'll ask the question: You said the most senior-ranking officer who was there. Who was the most senior-ranking officer who was there?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: The most senior-ranking officer was Mr. Sefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting, I agreed with Mr. Zuka to set off for reconnaissance the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you go back to Grabovica that night?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And when you went back to Grabovica, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I conveyed the conclusions from the meeting or the briefing to the company commanders -- actually, to the company commander and the platoon commanders, and I decided who would go out for reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then what -- how did the night end?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you do anything else or did you go to bed? I mean, let's finish the 8th.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We went to sleep so that we could prepare and be rested for the next day's assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So, now, the next day, being the 9th of September, 1993, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: That day I went for reconnaissance, and a part of the unit -- actually, with a part of the unit, three or four men, while the rest of the unit stayed in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who accompanied you to this reconnaissance other than your own company commanders.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Zuka was there. Pecar was there, on behalf of the 10th Mountain Brigade. I think his name was Senad Pecar. And another soldier was there. His name was Dzeki or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What time did you leave in the morning for reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Very early.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So did you return to Grabovica later that day?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We came back late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What time would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was about 10.00 or 11.00 at night. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When you arrived back at Grabovica, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I found my commander and deputy commander, who had arrived during the day to Grabovica, and I reported to them about what we did during the reconnaissance, and we agreed on what had to be done for the unit to move out on the deployment of the men. Simply we were preparing our combat assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said your commander, which is Adnan Solakovic, and his deputy, Samir Pezo -- are these the two that -- that had arrived in Grabovica that you alluded to earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: That night when I returned, they were there. It was the first time that I saw them, so they must have arrived at Grabovica in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you hear whether anybody else had arrived at Grabovica during the course of that day?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that members of the 9th Mountain Brigade had arrived and that they had been billeted in the same village as us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that night?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I was tired that night and I didn't hear anything, because I had walked more than 30 kilometres that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The next morning - that would be 10 September 1993 - what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: When we got up in the morning, one of our soldiers - I don't remember the name - came and said that he had found a body by the road. That road went through that village. And the soldier -- oh, and that it was the body of a soldier and that he wasn't from our unit and that they didn't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you -- sorry, one minute. And did you find out whose unit that particular soldier belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Later, we found out that it was a member of the Zuka's unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what ethnicity did this particular soldier belong to that you were informed about?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard from Zuka that he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, we had a meeting, small meeting, of the command and we decided to transfer all the members of our units of different or of other ethnic groups who were not out on combat assignment to our unit, to a different building for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why for their own safety?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the soldiers were upset because they had heard stories that some people from other units had asked for these people saying, "You have Serbs. You have Croats. They should be killed," and so on. But these were just stories. So in order to prevent anything like that from happening, we made the decision to act in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And did you do that? Did you secure your units?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document at this point, which is -- the 65 ter is 173, and it's 03343024. It will come up on the screen. If you look at the screen, it will soon be there.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a coded message.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right. Can you tell us about this coded message?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a message. I don't know how to read it. You would need a piece of paper in order to be able to read it. You would need to have the encryption code in order to be able to decipher this message.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is it not in the -- it has been deciphered, Your Honour. Is it not on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We don't have the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The English version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no, we don't have it. We just have two single numbers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm trying to clarify, whether we have the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to assist everyone, we have got the English version on the screen at the moment. I think -- I'm told by someone who knows about this that you have to go back to the main menu and then select the English channel and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Most importantly, does the witness have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you have the -- before you now in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Perhaps he could be assisted. English or B/C/S. I think the witness does speak English. That's fine. B/C/S is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who sent this message?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I have seen only one page of this message. Now I can see the other page. This is a message that was sent by our chief of communications and which was written by Adnan Solakovic as deputy commander and me. And I think that we signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So who were you sending this coded message to? The name, please.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We sent did to the commander of the 1st Corps, Vahid Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why did you feel the need to send a coded message at all?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that situation, we thought it best to send it to our immediate commander and to send the message in code because -- well, perhaps for our own personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Let's look at this message. You say in this: "We carried out a reconnaissance for three days, but it seems that the agreement with the chief is off." What agreement was this, "the agreement with the chief is off"?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think this refers to the problem of resubordination of the unit under the command of Zulfikar. I think that's what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the chief here would be who? Who are you referring to by "chief"?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Mr. Sefer probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: "The operation is being postponed more and more. We have the order until Sunday, but it seems that it is off. Strange things are happening. I am afraid for my soldiers, who are of a different religion." What were these strange things which were happening?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think the "strange things" refers to the murders that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which murders may these be?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the first soldier was killed, the one I've already mentioned, the member of Zuka's unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Had you heard about other murders by the time you wrote this coded message, other than the soldier that you mention?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had already heard about five or six dead bodies that were found in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you go on to say: "People are simply disappearing over night." And then you say: "Send us back into town any which you can. If it is necessary, go to the head. Let him make up a reason for the return," et cetera. Then you say: "The chief put us under the command of Zuka." Now, the "chief" here refers to, again, who?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: To Mr. Sefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then you say: "I'm afraid that a conflict between us might occur." What kind of a conflict were you alluding to there, and between who?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We were afraid that the people who had already murdered those civilians might go on killing and that they might kill the members of our unit who were of a different religion. That's what this refers to. And, of course, we would defend our men, and then we would enter into a mutual conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then you plead: "Do that as soon as possible. I do not want to take part in these dirty games, and it is not as you were told." What dirty games were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is a metaphor of sorts to avoid saying what had happened directly. We didn't know who would be reading this coded message. What we meant was we didn't want to participate in events in a place where such things were going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you get a response to this coded message of yours?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We never received any reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you report this to anyone else other than Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Not me, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why was that? Why did you not go to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: After our return to town, things happened very quickly and no one had time to discuss it or the inclination to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But while you were on the ground in Herzegovina at the time you sent this coded message to your corps commander, there were other people around in the area, in the region. Did you tell this to Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at a very low level compared to Sefer Halilovic. I wasn't even a commander. It was up to my commander to do it. And whether he did it or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to let the record show that will be MFI272. The coded message, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, if it's being tendered, I don't object. Is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Since there is no objection, this document is tendered into evidence. And how about the first document we used?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which would be MFI270, Your Honour, and I would tender that into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought that that was already in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I -- from the transcript, I do not see that the Prosecution was tendering that document into evidence, so I just reminded her about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, yes. Sorry. Well, I can just say there is no objection to the report that the witness referred to, and there was no objection to the photograph also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those documents, I believe three of them, are admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I normally would do it at the end of my evidence. I mean, that's -- but I can always do it as we go along as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Okovic. Can we -- can I ask you that -- you did not go to Sefer Halilovic, but do you know whether -- whether Solakovic, Adnan Solakovic, went to him?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now we're still on the 10th of September, 1993. And what did you do after you sent this coded report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I just wasn't sure that the witness ever said that it was sent on the 10th, Your Honours, and I'm not sure whether that's the fact or not. That should be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we should establish that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When did you send this report? It is dated --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, 11th is the next day. Right. Sorry, Your Honours. I'll just go back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do on the 10th, after you were told that this soldier has been killed and you had secured your units? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, part of the unit, as I said, and as far as I can recall, was transferred to Dreznica. There were some problems about transportation, and we spent the whole day doing that. And then when we heard about what had happened down there, we sent this message. It was sometime in the afternoon, late afternoon. I don't know exactly when, but I think I saw on the message it said 1730 hours. If this is the authentic document, then that's correct. But I am sure it was in the afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Did you go anywhere yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think we went or that I went to the mountains again. I'm not sure about the date, but I think I went to Prenj again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who did you go to Prenj with?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: With Zuka.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did Zuka come to Grabovica or you went to meet Zuka somewhere else before you went to Prenj?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: He came -- he came to collect me in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at Prenj?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We spent that night there, the two of us, at Prenj because the artillery roster was being drawn up and the units were already ready to move.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What time did Zuka arrive at the village in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the morning quite early, but I can't tell you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did he do anything else while he was in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. So, now, you spent the night of the 10th September 1999 in Prenj. What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the dates are correct, but after spending the night at Prenj, the operation started. And it was interrupted sometime late in the afternoon, and that's when we returned to Grabovica, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who brought you back to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there was a vehicle waiting for us down there, because we descended along the rocks. We didn't go the long way around. We came down very quickly from the command post. It wasn't night yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what did you do when you arrived back at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: There I found -- Zuka left me there. I don't think he even came close to our camp. And there I found my commander, the deputy commander, and Caco and some of his men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you -- did they say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were enjoying themselves, having fun.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard from the men -- because I didn't want to join the company sitting there, so he heard from some of the men who were in the house on the other side, and they told me the whole story of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: That a lot of people had been killed in the village, women, children, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did they tell you who these people were, what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: They were Croats by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you told who killed them?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ask?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, nobody would certainly have told me, even if I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What else did you inquire about, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked the commander that we should withdraw from this operation as soon as possible, and he wanted the same thing, but circumstances were different and this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So was it on this day that -- and that's what the report says, your coded message of the 11th September -- that's when you sent your message that we've already looked at?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there anything missing from any of the houses which had been kept there?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing was missing from the houses we were in except that they told me Zuka had sent some men to take away a Croatian couple, to take them to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there a chapel in the cemetery where you were that something happened to?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I heard several explosions, and I asked what was going on there. Nobody replied. It was only later on that I learned that the Catholic chapel had been destroyed and that some graves had been destroyed in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Did you do anything else on that day? That's 11 September 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that on that day, together with the commander, we attended a meeting at Zuka's, in his base.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was that on the 11th or was that the next day, on the 12th? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'm not sure. That is, I don't know if it was the same day or the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you went, you say, to Zuka's base?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who else went with you?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I went with Commander Solakovic, and our security officer went along too, Pike.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was there when you got there? Who did you find there?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Zuka was there, Ramiz Delalic, and Mr. Sefer. I don't remember whether anyone else was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you attend this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were you told what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander conveyed to us that he had asked that we should withdraw and that the operation should be ended, but that this proposal had not been accepted. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And by whom was it not accepted?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably by the people who were at the meeting. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a convenient point to break, if that's -- oh, should we go at 4.20? I just got a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a break that might be shorter. We will take a 20-minute break, and we will resume at quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Okovic, before the break we were talking about the meeting at Zuka's base. What did you do after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting, we - that is, the commander and the security officer - we were returning to the base in Grabovica. We came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did anything happen when you came back?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: As we were leaving the tunnel, before turning off toward the bridge leading to the right bank of the river where we were billeted in Grabovica, we saw some people and we stopped there. Something was happening. When we stopped the vehicle and got out, we found Caco there and a soldier - I don't know whether it was one of his men or somebody from another unit - and a civilian. Caco was trying to set fire to the dead body of an old man who might have been between 70 and 80. And then I said to him, "How would you feel if somebody was trying to set fire to your father like that?" And he said, "You want me to set fire to you too?" He asked us to give him some fuel from the car so he could douse the body with gasoline, but we did not do this. Then he made the civilian go and find some petrol or oil so that he could pour it over the body and set it on fire. The commander said that we should leave, and so we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before we go on, who is Caco?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: "Caco" is Musan Topalovic's nickname. He was the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you see this body on fire?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't manage to set it on fire while we were there, but the man had already been dead for some time. I didn't see who had killed him, but he was trying to set fire to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this civilian who was there, what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you try to stop him?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't have been a wise thing to do at that point in time for any of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why would it not have been a wise thing to do?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Because Caco was that kind of person. He was ready to do anything, and it wasn't wise to get into any kind of conflict with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Had you heard about Caco before that time?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What had you heard about him?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, he was a good fighter. But as the war went on, I heard a lot of bad things about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there anybody else that you heard bad things about as the war continued?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: I was only in town then, and I heard that in his area of responsibility there were murders and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where did you go after you -- after this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC
utterances.text: We went to the base, to Grabovica, to our command in the village of Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what did you do there?
